children: , the semiconductor-production equipment leader, turned India's semiconductor push into a $5 billion, decade-long bet on research, suppliers and talent, Reuters reported Thursday. The shares traded around $416.40, up roughly 0.3% based on the earlier reference level. The valuation picture is much hotter than the stock move: GuruFocus data shows the market price sitting 68.39% above GF Value of $247.28, signaling that investors are already paying a hefty premium for future growth.

The spending plan works out to roughly $500 million a year and targets the infrastructure India still needs to become a serious chip-manufacturing hub. The opportunity is enormous on paper. India expects semiconductor consumption to reach $110 billion by 2030, up from roughly $45 billion to $50 billion in 2025. But there is still a major gap between demand and manufacturing depth. Three packaging plants are operating, while a large-scale fabrication ecosystem has yet to fully emerge.

For Applied, this is a measured wager rather than a balance-sheet gamble. The annualized commitment equals only about 1.4% of revenue based on its record $9.12 billion quarterly sales, giving the company room to build an early position without letting India dominate capital allocation. The real payoff comes if government incentives translate into actual fabsand those fabs start ordering deposition, etch and other production tools at scale. With the shares already priced far above GF Value, execution in India will matter more than the headline size of the commitment.

title: Applied Materials Edged Higher Behind a $5 Billion India Buildout
